name: Marcus Reyes
what it tests: The clean case. Specific answers at every turn - this is the ceiling.
problem: Every Thursday I spend about three hours pulling numbers for the Friday pipeline review - same twelve accounts, same slides, and half of it is retyping what Salesforce already knows.
step 4 action: Write the summary email to my director
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, rebuilding the slides. Same twelve layouts every week with new numbers dropped in, and it eats an hour and a half on its own.
chat 2a output: One slide per account: account name, quarter-to-date number against target, the two deals most likely to close, and one line on risk. Same order every week, no more than 40 words per slide.
chat 2b keep: The risk line. That is my read on the account from calls I have had, and it is the only part my director actually reads closely.
chat 3 context: Never estimate a number - if a field is blank in the export, write MISSING and leave it. Account names must match Salesforce exactly including the Inc and LLC suffixes. Anything above 250k needs a legal review flag.

name: Dana Whitcomb
what it tests: The vague case. Every answer is mush. Does the activity produce something honest about that, or something that only looks finished?
problem: I spend way too long every month writing up our grant reports and it is basically the same thing each time.
step 1 action: Gather program numbers from the team
chat 1 handoff: Probably the writing part. It just takes forever.
chat 2a output: Just something that sounds professional and is not so dry.
chat 2b keep: I do not know, I guess the parts about impact?
chat 3 context: Not really anything, just make it good.
retry 1: The narrative section, step 2. I want a first draft I can edit.
retry 2a: I do not know really, just better than what I write now.
retry 2b: The impact stories. Those come from site visits and I write those myself.

name: Amara Osei
what it tests: The over-handover case. Chat 1 offers up the judgment call; chat 2 takes it back. Does the finished prompt end up coherent or self-contradicting?
problem: Every week I write screening summaries for people who contacted us about the diabetes trial - about fifteen a week, and I am copying the same eligibility language over and over.
step 2 action: Check each against inclusion and exclusion criteria
chat 1 handoff: Honestly all of it. Step 2 especially - checking criteria is just matching a list.
chat 2a output: One paragraph per candidate, plain language, stating which criteria they meet and which they do not. No more than 150 words.
chat 2b keep: The final eligible or not eligible call. That has to be me - it goes in the regulatory file with my name on it.
chat 3 context: Never infer a value that was not in the questionnaire - if something is missing, say MISSING. Never use the participant name, only the study ID. And it must never state that someone is eligible, only whether the criteria are met.

name: Priya Raghavan
what it tests: Clean run in a shift-work setting. Short workflow, hard constraints.
problem: Every day I get twenty or so shift swap requests by text and email, and I have to check each one against the roster rules before I can say yes or no.
step 1 action: Collect the swap requests from text and email
step 2 action: Check each against the roster rules
step 3 action: Reply to the nurse and update the roster
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, checking each request against the rules. It is the same seven rules every time and I do it twenty times a day.
chat 2a output: For each request: the two names, the two shifts, which rules it passes, which it fails, and a one-line plain-English reason. No more than 60 words each.
chat 2b keep: The final yes or no. Some of these are close calls about fairness and I have to own that with my staff.
chat 3 context: Never guess at a rule. If a shift is missing from the roster export, write MISSING and stop. Use the badge number, not the name, in anything you write back.

name: Tomás Herrera
what it tests: Non-desk job, physical inventory, supplier ordering.
problem: Every Sunday night I count inventory and put in five supplier orders, and I spend two hours rebuilding the same order sheets from last week with different numbers.
step 1 action: Count what is on the shelves
step 3 action: Build the order for each of five suppliers
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, building the five order sheets. Once I know the counts it is just arithmetic against par and I have done it wrong when I am tired.
chat 2a output: One order sheet per supplier, their item codes in their order, quantity and unit only. No prices. Flag anything I am ordering more than 30 percent above last week.
chat 2b keep: Anything perishable. I decide how much produce to buy based on what the weather is doing and how the weekend went.
chat 3 context: Never round quantities up to a case unless the supplier only sells cases. Sysco item codes are seven digits, the others are five. If a par level is blank, write MISSING.

name: Lena Fischer
what it tests: Templated documents with legal exposure.
problem: I write about eight offer letters a month and each one is the same document with the salary, title, start date and equity swapped out, plus whatever the hiring manager negotiated.
step 2 action: Draft the letter from our template
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, drafting the letter. The template is fixed, it is just filling it correctly and getting the negotiated bits worded right.
chat 2a output: Our standard letter, exactly the template order, with the six variable fields filled. Under one page. Formal but not stiff.
chat 2b keep: Anything about the equity grant. That wording has been through legal and I do not improvise on it.
chat 3 context: Never invent a start date - if it is not in the approved terms, write MISSING. Job titles must match the requisition exactly. Never mention bonus eligibility unless the terms include it.

name: Wesley Okafor
what it tests: Public-facing writing with a compliance edge.
problem: I send about forty permit status letters a week and they are the same six paragraphs with a different address, permit number and reason for delay.
step 2 action: Work out which status letter applies
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, writing the letter. There are six templates and I know which one applies by the time I get there.
chat 2a output: Formal letter, our four-paragraph structure, plain language at about an eighth grade reading level. Under 250 words. Always ends with the appeal window.
chat 2b keep: Any letter that involves a code violation. Those can end up in front of a hearing officer and I write those myself.
chat 3 context: Never state a decision the record does not show. Permit numbers are formatted BLD-YYYY-NNNN. If the delay reason field is empty, write MISSING rather than guessing.

name: Aditi Sharma
what it tests: Synthesis rather than templating - summarising many items into themes.
problem: Every Friday I read through the week’s support tickets and write up the top themes for the product team, which takes me most of an afternoon.
step 2 action: Group them into themes by hand
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, the grouping. I am reading four hundred tickets and sorting them into maybe eight buckets, and that is the part that eats the afternoon.
chat 2a output: Eight themes maximum, each with a count, two representative ticket IDs, and one sentence on what the customer was actually trying to do. Ranked by count.
chat 2b keep: The recommendation at the end about what product should fix first. That is a judgement call about our roadmap and it is mine.
chat 3 context: Never merge two themes that have different root causes just because the wording is similar. Use ticket IDs, never customer names. If a ticket has no resolution note, leave it out and say how many you left out.

name: Colm Byrne
what it tests: Numeric comparison work where a mistake is expensive.
problem: For every project I get five to nine subcontractor bids in different formats and I have to normalise them into one comparison sheet before I can recommend anything.
step 2 action: Pull the line items into a common format
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, normalising the line items. Every sub formats their bid differently and I am retyping the same twelve trades into my sheet.
chat 2a output: One row per trade, one column per bidder, dollars only. A separate list of anything a bidder excluded that others included. No commentary.
chat 2b keep: The recommendation. Price is only half of it and the other half is whether I trust the crew to show up.
chat 3 context: Never total a column that has a missing bid in it. Alternates are not base bid - keep them separate. If a bid has no date, write MISSING.

name: Ruth Delgado
what it tests: Education data with student privacy constraints.
problem: Every Monday I flag students whose attendance has dropped and write a short note to each school so they can follow up, about thirty notes a week.
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, writing the notes. It is the same three sentences per student and I write thirty of them.
chat 2a output: One short paragraph per school listing the flagged students by ID, their current rate against their average, and the drop. No more than 100 words per school.
chat 2b keep: Anything about why a student might be absent. I do not speculate and neither should this.
chat 3 context: Never use a student name, only the state ID. Never suggest a cause for the absence. If attendance data is incomplete for a week, say MISSING and do not calculate an average from partial data.

name: Brett Halloran
what it tests: Vague and busy. Not evasive, just has never had to specify anything.
problem: I spend my evenings answering customer emails and it eats my whole night, every night.
chat 1 handoff: The emails. All of it really.
chat 2a output: Just professional. Something that sounds like me but faster.
chat 2b keep: I mean I should probably check them.
chat 3 context: Not really. Just do it right.
retry 1: Step 2, writing back. Mostly quotes and scheduling.
retry 2a: Short. Two or three sentences, friendly, no jargon.
retry 2b: Anything with a price in it. I want to see those before they go.
retry 3: Never quote a price. Leave a blank for it and I will fill it in.

name: Sofia Marchetti
what it tests: Vague AND subjective - "on brand" is the whole spec in her head.
problem: I write social captions for three channels every week and it takes forever to make them not sound the same.
step 1 action: Get the week’s content from the team
chat 1 handoff: The writing. Obviously.
chat 2a output: On brand. You know, our voice.
chat 2b keep: Hmm. I guess anything sensitive?
chat 3 context: Not that I can think of.
retry 1: Step 2. I want first drafts for each channel that I can then cut down.
retry 2a: Instagram under 125 characters, LinkedIn two short paragraphs, no hashtags anywhere. Never use an exclamation mark.
retry 2b: Anything about a customer story. Those need their approval and I handle that.
retry 3: Never name a client unless I have put the name in the brief. No emoji in LinkedIn.

name: Gerald Whitmore
what it tests: Vague and stays vague. Both pushbacks fail - the marked-prompt path.
problem: The paperwork side of renewals takes up way more of my week than it should.
chat 1 handoff: The paperwork part.
chat 2a output: Better than what I do now.
chat 2b keep: Not sure.
chat 3 context: Nothing really comes to mind.
retry 2b: I would have to think about it.

name: Nadia Hassan
what it tests: Vague, and the good answer is genuinely hard to articulate.
problem: I write listing descriptions for every property and after ten years they all sound identical to me.
step 1 action: Walk the property and take notes
step 2 action: Pull the specs from the MLS sheet
chat 1 handoff: The writing bit.
chat 2a output: Something that actually sells the place.
chat 2b keep: I do not know really.
chat 3 context: Just make it sound good.
retry 1: Step 3. A first draft from my walkthrough notes and the specs.
retry 2a: Under 200 words, no more than two adjectives in a row, leads with the thing that is actually unusual about the house.
retry 2b: Anything about the neighbourhood or schools. Fair housing rules and I will not risk it.
retry 3: Never mention schools, demographics, or who would like the house. Never say a square footage that is not on the MLS sheet.

name: Julian Feldman
what it tests: Offers up the legal judgement in chat 1, pulls it back in chat 2.
problem: I summarise deposition transcripts for the attorneys, about four a month, and each one is three hundred pages I have to boil down to two.
step 4 action: Flag anything that contradicts an earlier deposition
chat 1 handoff: All of it honestly. Especially step 4, contradiction spotting is just comparing two documents.
chat 2a output: Two pages maximum, chronological, every point cited to a page and line number. No characterisation, just what was said.
chat 2b keep: Calling something a contradiction. That is a legal judgement and if I am wrong an attorney walks into a deposition with bad information.
chat 3 context: Never paraphrase testimony without the page and line cite. Never infer what a witness meant. If a passage is unclear, quote it and say it is unclear.

name: Hana Kimura
what it tests: Sweeping handoff on something with patient-safety consequences.
problem: I prepare the daily med reconciliation lists for the pharmacist and I am transcribing the same fields off intake forms fifty times a day.
step 4 action: Build the reconciliation sheet for the pharmacist
chat 1 handoff: Everything. Step 3 especially, interaction checking is a lookup table.
chat 2a output: One row per medication: name, dose, route, frequency, source. Anything that differs between the two lists highlighted. Nothing else.
chat 2b keep: The clinical call on whether an interaction actually matters for this patient. That is the pharmacist’s and I do not touch it.
chat 3 context: Never infer a dose that is not written down. Never expand an abbreviation you are not certain of - flag it. Never say a drug is safe or unsafe, only that the lists differ.

name: Owen Fitzgerald
what it tests: Wants the approve/decline call automated, then admits it cannot be.
problem: I write credit memos for every loan application and it is the same eight sections every time with different numbers in them.
step 1 action: Pull the financials and credit report
chat 1 handoff: The whole memo, and honestly step 4 too. The ratios tell you the answer.
chat 2a output: Our eight-section memo, in order, ratios shown to two decimal places with the inputs beside them. Under three pages.
chat 2b keep: The recommendation. It goes to committee with my name on it and there is always something the ratios do not show.
chat 3 context: Never calculate a ratio from an incomplete statement - say MISSING. Never characterise the borrower. Never state a recommendation, only the figures.

name: Margaret Oyelaran
what it tests: Wants to keep every step. Tests whether the activity can produce anything useful when the honest answer is "not much".
problem: I write progress notes after every session, about twenty five a week, and it adds an hour to every day.
step 2 action: Update the treatment plan if needed
chat 1 handoff: Honestly none of it. Every word of a progress note is clinical judgement and it is a legal record.
chat 2a output: If it did anything it would just be the structure - our note format with the headings and nothing filled in.
chat 2b keep: All of the content. Every observation, every intervention, every assessment.
chat 3 context: Never write clinical content. Never infer a diagnosis. Never put anything in a note that I did not say happened.

name: Desmond Clarke
what it tests: Refuses the premise, sceptically. Tests the tone when the learner pushes back on the activity itself.
problem: I spend a full day a week just organising interview notes and documents so I can find things later.
step 2 action: Tag documents by source and topic
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, the tagging. That is filing, not journalism. Nothing else.
chat 2a output: Tags only. Source, date, topic, and whether it is on the record. No summaries, no interpretation.
chat 2b keep: Everything else. The chronology is where I work out what the story is and I am not outsourcing that.
chat 3 context: Never summarise a document. Never characterise a source. Never merge two sources into one entry. If a date is ambiguous, tag it unknown.

name: Yuki Tanaka
what it tests: Almost no software. Tests what the tools field does when the honest answer is paper.
problem: Every morning I go through yesterday’s paper intake forms and type them into the system, about thirty forms.
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, the typing. It is transcription and I make mistakes when I rush it.
chat 2a output: One record per form, our field order, exactly what is written on the form. Anything illegible marked, not guessed.
chat 2b keep: Anything in the notes field about the animal’s condition. If the vet wrote it I want to read it myself.
chat 3 context: Never expand an abbreviation. Never clean up a phone number, type what is written. If handwriting is unclear, write UNCLEAR and move on.

name: Fabien Roux
what it tests: Seven workflow steps. Tests the step builder and how a long list reads in the finished prompt.
problem: Every shipment I book goes through the same seven-step paper trail, and a full booking takes forty minutes of copying the same details between systems.
chat 1 handoff: Step 6, the confirmation pack. Six documents that all say the same thing in different boxes.
chat 2a output: The six standard documents, our field order, every reference number matching the booking exactly. No prose.
chat 2b keep: The customs classification. Get that wrong and it is my licence, not a delayed box.
chat 3 context: Never invent an HS code. Never round a weight. Container numbers are four letters then seven digits, and if one does not match that, stop and flag it.

name: Grace Ampofo
what it tests: Only two workflow steps, the minimum the activity accepts.
problem: Every month end I categorise about four hundred transactions across six clients and it is the same categories every time.
chat 1 handoff: Step 2. Ninety percent of them are the same twenty vendors every month.
chat 2a output: One line per transaction with a proposed category and a confidence level. Anything below high confidence goes in a separate list for me.
chat 2b keep: Anything I have not seen before, and anything over five hundred pounds. Those I look at myself.
chat 3 context: Never create a new category. Never split a transaction. If a vendor is new, put it in the review list rather than guessing.

name: Ivan Petrov
what it tests: A very long problem statement. Tests how a wall of text renders and carries into the prompt.
problem: Every quarter I put together the compliance reporting pack for three funding bodies, and each one wants the same underlying information in a different structure with different terminology, so I end up rewriting the same fifteen facts three times over, plus there is a safety section that overlaps with our internal audit but not exactly, and the deadlines are two weeks apart which means I do it three times rather than once, and by the third one I have usually lost track of which version has the corrected headcount in it.
step 3 action: Cross-check the three against each other
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, writing the three reports from one set of figures. Same facts, three structures.
chat 2a output: Three documents, each in that funder’s section order and their terminology. Every figure identical across all three. No narrative beyond what each section asks for.
chat 2b keep: The safety section. That has my signature on it and I write it once, carefully, myself.
chat 3 context: Never let a figure differ between the three reports. If a figure is provisional, say so in every report it appears in. Never use one funder’s terminology in another’s document.

name: Bilal Karim
what it tests: Terse throughout, but genuinely specific. Tests whether the vagueness check fires on brevity alone.
problem: I write up ticket resolutions at the end of every day. Thirty tickets, the same six sentence shapes.
chat 1 handoff: Step 2. Draft note per ticket.
chat 2a output: Four lines: symptom, cause, fix, prevention. Under 60 words. No jargon.
chat 2b keep: Root cause when it is a guess. I mark those myself.
chat 3 context: Never state a cause the ticket does not evidence. Asset tags are six digits. A missing field means MISSING.

name: Rosa Jiménez
what it tests: Answers questions with questions. Tests what happens when the learner will not commit.
problem: I write degree audit summaries for students, about forty a term, explaining what they still need in order to graduate.
step 2 action: Work out what is still outstanding
step 3 action: Write the summary for the student
chat 1 handoff: What would you suggest? Probably the writing?
chat 2a output: What does a good one usually look like for something like this?
chat 2b keep: What do most people keep?
chat 3 context: Is there anything I should be worried about here?
retry 1: Step 3 then. The summary email, from the audit output.
retry 2a: Plain language, under 200 words, a bulleted list of what is left and how many credits each one is.
retry 2b: Any advice about what to take next term. That is a conversation, not an email.
retry 3: Never tell a student they will graduate on a date. Never mention financial aid. If the audit has an exception on it, say to come and see me.

name: Simone Aubert
what it tests: Craft work where good is genuinely contested. Tests whether an output spec can carry taste.
problem: I write wall labels for every object in a show, two hundred labels, and each one has to say the same kind of thing in fifty words.
step 4 action: Send to the curator for review
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, a first draft of each label from the curator notes and the object record.
chat 2a output: Exactly fifty words. One idea per label. No art-historical jargon, no masterpiece, no rhetorical questions. Present tense.
chat 2b keep: The opening sentence. That is what a visitor reads in the two seconds they give me, and I write those.
chat 3 context: Never state a date or attribution that is not in the object record. If the record says attributed to, the label must say it too. Never describe what the artist was feeling.

name: Theo Nkemelu
what it tests: Creative-adjacent, but with a hard format spec.
problem: Every episode needs show notes, timestamps and three social pull-quotes, and it takes me longer than the edit does.
chat 1 handoff: Steps 2 and 4, the summary and the quote pulls. Timestamps I do while editing anyway.
chat 2a output: Summary under 120 words in second person. Three quotes, each under 25 words, verbatim from the transcript with a timestamp.
chat 2b keep: Which quotes actually go out. The best line for the show is not always the best line in the episode.
chat 3 context: Quotes must be word for word, never tidied up. Never quote the ad read. If a guest asked for something off the record it is not in the transcript, so never fill gaps.

name: Bridget Nolan
what it tests: Evaluative writing where consistency between reviewers is the whole point.
problem: I score about sixty applications a round and write a scoring narrative for each one against five criteria.
step 3 action: Write the narrative for each score
chat 1 handoff: Step 3, the narrative. The score is mine, but writing out why in the house style takes as long as reading the thing.
chat 2a output: One paragraph per criterion, 60 to 80 words, quoting the application where it evidences the score. Neutral tone, no praise language.
chat 2b keep: The scores themselves. Every one of them.
chat 3 context: Never suggest a score. Never compare one applicant to another. Only quote what is in the application, and if a criterion is not addressed, say it is not addressed.

name: Anders Lindqvist
what it tests: Airworthiness records. The strictest guardrails in the set.
problem: Every check I plan generates the same work package paperwork, and I spend a day and a half transcribing task numbers between three systems.
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, building the package from the due list. It is assembly, not engineering judgement.
chat 2a output: One line per task: task number, revision, zone, estimated hours, required qualification. In task number order. Nothing else.
chat 2b keep: Anything involving a deferral. Deferring a task is a signed engineering decision and it is mine.
chat 3 context: Never transcribe a task number without its revision letter. Never combine two tasks. If the programme revision does not match the task revision, stop and flag it rather than resolving it.

name: Cheryl Boateng
what it tests: The highest-stakes case in the set, where the right answer is that most of it stays human.
problem: I write court report summaries for every case going to review, about twelve a month, and each one pulls from six months of case notes.
chat 1 handoff: Step 2, the chronology. Dates, contact type, who was present. It is extraction from what I already wrote.
chat 2a output: A table: date, contact type, participants, whether it was announced. Chronological. No narrative, no summary of what happened.
chat 2b keep: Every word of the assessment. What the contacts mean for this child is the entire job, and it goes to a judge under my name.
chat 3 context: Never characterise a contact. Never infer why a visit did not happen. Use initials, never full names of children. If a note is missing for a scheduled contact, show the gap rather than closing it.
